wa_headlight_point.blurb: Headlight Point is a small cliff in the Exit 38 climbing zone beside Interstate 90 near North Bend, up the hillside from the Dirty Harry's Peak trailhead lot. Of its 22 routes, most are bolted sport lines and a handful are trad, spanning 5.6 to the low 5.11s with the bulk between 5.6 and 5.10. The routes are short and follow juggy flakes, and the wall steepens toward one end. A few brief multi-pitch lines look out over the highway corridor. It faces the morning, dries quickly, and can catch strong wind funnelling along the valley. Traffic noise carries up, and the gully beside the crag sheds loose rock.

wa_eastern_block.blurb: Eastern Block is one of the bigger crags in the Interstate Park group of the Exit 38 area, close to Interstate 90 near North Bend, and it sits beside Headlight Point. All 21 routes are bolted sport climbs. The grades are moderate to mid-range: a single 5.7, then a cluster of 5.8s, several 5.9s and 5.10s, and a few 5.11s at the top. It makes a good stop for a climber who wants a varied day of intermediate leads. The crag is open to the morning light, dries out fast after rain, and can be hit by wind coming down the valley.

wa_roman_boulder.blurb: Roman Boulder is the first big block you meet where the main trail ends in the Empire Boulders, a bouldering zone in the Columbia Gorge on the Washington side. It holds 21 problems and covers a wide range: a couple of beginner-friendly lines at the VB and V0 level, a solid middle tier up to about V3, and then a block of much harder problems reaching into double-digit V grades. The boulder has a large slabby face on one side and another face cut by a water groove, so there is a bit of variety in style. Bring a pad; the easy problems make it a good place for a mixed group.

wa_roadside_rock_east.blurb: Roadside Rock East is the east-side section of a granite formation next to Highway 155 at Banks Lake in central Washington. Of its 21 problems and routes, 19 are bolted sport climbs and two are boulder problems. The sport grades run from about 5.6 to 5.12, with most in the 5.9 to 5.11 range, so it suits climbers working the middle grades and up. A gravel pullout puts you close to the rock, and a short trail drops down to its base. Watch for poison ivy along the path and the occasional wasp nest in the flakes.

wa_martian_slabs.blurb: Martian Slabs is the most visible formation as you walk up toward the spires of Peshastin Pinnacles State Park, near Leavenworth. It is mostly low-angle friction climbing, with 21 routes: 13 trad and 8 sport. Grades start around 5.5 and run through the 5.8 to 5.10 range, with a couple of 5.11 bolted lines for stronger climbers. The base is a short walk up a maintained trail from the lot. The park can get quite hot in summer, so plan an early start or a cooler time of year, and bring shoes you trust on smooth rock.

wa_beach_the.blurb: The Beach is a sector at Index Town Walls in the Skykomish valley, on the east end of the Upper Cheeks, where a wide ledge system begins that gives the sector its name. It holds 21 routes, a mix of 14 sport, 6 trad and one aid line. This is hard climbing: only one route is below 5.10, most sit between 5.10 and 5.12, and a few go beyond that. The Upper Cheeks is known for steep, clean, exposed rock that stays relatively dry, so it is a place for experienced climbers comfortable on overhanging terrain, reached by traversing along the base of the wall.
